claims.claim: Motion in the slow axis results in whole lines of the sample being sampled either twice or not at all.
claims.source: this is unsurprising as motion in the slow axis will result in whole lines of the sample being sampled either twice or not at all.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the raster scan pattern used in laser scanning microscopy.

claims.claim: The range of amplitudes and frequencies that Galene is able to correct covers a broad range of physiologically relevant motions commonly observed during functional intravital imaging.
claims.source: We note that the range of amplitudes and frequencies that Galene is able to correct covers a broad range of physiologically relevant motions commonly observed during functional intravital imaging and will therefore be of use in a range of in vivo imaging applications.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 2 compared to physiological motion parameters.

claims.claim: Galene can correct for a significantly larger range of motions than StackReg, SIFT, and SIMA packages.
claims.source: However, Galene is able to correct for significantly larger sample motions than SIMA (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1Aiv, SIMA and v, Galene), for example the larger motion shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, corresponding to a larger motion induced by the heartbeat, and so will be useful in a broader range of intravital experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: StackReg and SIFT are only able to correct for low frequency motion as they correct for rigid transformations between frames.
claims.source: StackReg and SIFT both correct for rigid transformations between each frame and so are unable to cope with the distortion produced by LSM with a moving sample; consequently, these packages are only able to correct for low frequency motion (as, for example, encountered during slow sample drifts where the observed motion artefact can be approximated by a linear transformation (for example, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: SIMA uses a HMM model which uses information about the laser scan pattern and is able to cope with a larger range of motion than StackReg and SIFT.
claims.source: SIMA uses a HMM model which uses information about the laser scan pattern and so is able to cope with a larger range of motion (for example, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, equivalent to a small displacement caused by the heartbeat).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Titanium windows enable longitudinal imaging of abdominal organs.
claims.source: We acquired images through surgically implanted titanium windows (see schematic in Figure 3) that enable longitudinal imaging of abdominal organs (Ritsma et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ritsma et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Imaging abdominal organs through an optical window is challenging as they experience considerable motion as a result of physiological activity in nearby organs such as respiration and the heartbeat.
claims.source: Imaging abdominal organs through an optical window is challenging as they experience considerable motion as a result of physiological activity in nearby organs such as respiration and the heartbeat.
claims.evidence: This is based on practical experience and knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Finding areas sufficiently stable to acquire FLIM images through optical windows significantly limits the usable area of the window.
claims.source: Simply finding areas sufficiently stable to acquire FLIM images significantly limits the usable area of the window, and, in some cases, can render mice completely unusable.
claims.evidence: This is based on practical experience described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Motion dominated by the heartbeat has a frequency of 5.4 Hz and peak-peak amplitude of 27 μm (approximately 10% of the FOV) in pancreatic tissue imaging.
claims.source: We performed an amplitude-spectrum analysis on the estimated displacements (Figure 3B,C) and found motion of (i) a frequency of 5.4 Hz and peak-peak amplitude of 27 μm (approximately 10% of the FOV), corresponding to the heartbeat
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: Motion dominated by respiration and peristalsis has frequencies from 0.2 to 2.2 Hz with an average peak-peak amplitude of 42 μm (approximately 15% of the field of view) in pancreatic tissue imaging.
claims.source: and (ii) slower motions with a range of frequencies from 0.2 to 2.2 Hz with an average peak-peak amplitude of 42 μm (approximately 15% of the field of view), corresponding to respiration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: For faster but smaller motion due to the heartbeat, Galene can correct for motion equally well at all scan rates tested (700, 1000, and 1400 Hz).
claims.source: We found that for the faster but smaller motion due to the heartbeat we were able to correct for motion equally well at all scan rates (see Figure 3D, average correlation quantified in Figure 3Div).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: For larger motion due to respiration and peristalsis, successful correction was only obtained at 1400 Hz scan rates, with partial correction at 1000 Hz and effectively no correction at 700 Hz.
claims.source: For the larger due to respiration and peristalsis, we found that we were only able to successfully correct for motion at 1400 Hz scan rates; partial correction was obtained at 1000 Hz and effectively no correction at 700 Hz (see Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: For larger motions it may be helpful to acquire at a faster frame rate where possible.
claims.source: Underscoring the simulated data results, these data indicate that for larger motions it may be helpful to acquire at a faster frame rate where possible.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing better correction at higher scan rates for larger motions.

claims.claim: At 700 Hz, realignment is significantly improved when motion is aligned with the fast axis compared to the slow axis.
claims.source: At 700 Hz the realignment is significantly improved when the motion is aligned with the fast axis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: At 1400 Hz, motion is corrected equally well whether aligned with the fast or slow axis.
claims.source: At 1400 Hz, when the motion is slower relative to the scan rate, the motion is corrected equally well in either case.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: It is important to use a fast scan rate where possible for motion correction.
claims.source: This highlights both the importance of using a fast scan rate where possible and, where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing the effect of scan rate on correction quality.

claims.claim: Where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view can improve correction.
claims.source: This highlights both the importance of using a fast scan rate where possible and, where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing the effect of motion direction on correction quality.

claims.claim: There was a slight improvement in the average correlation with increasing number of realignment points up to 20 points for 256 × 256 images.
claims.source: For images of this size, there was a slight improvement in the average correlation with increasing number of realignment points up to 20 points.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Using 40 realignment points, the correlation was slightly reduced compared to 20 points for 256 × 256 images.
claims.source: Using 40 points, however, the correlation was slightly reduced.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Using a very large number of realignment points can be detrimental as there is not enough information to accurately determine the motion at each point.
claims.source: Using a very large number of realignment points can be detrimental; as the number of points increases, the number of pixels which constrain each point is reduced and eventually there is not enough information to accurately determine the motion at each point.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the nature of the optimization problem.

claims.claim: Using between 5–20 realignment points for 256 × 256 images and 10–20 points for 512 × 512 images was sufficient to obtain good correction over a broad range of conditions.
claims.source: In general, we found that using between 5–20 realignment points for 256 × 256 images and 10–20 points for 512 × 512 images was sufficient to obtain good correction over a broad range of conditions.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical testing described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A Gaussian smoothing kernel may optionally be applied to each frame before realignment to improve the realignment when signal to noise level is low.
claims.source: As the signal to noise level in each frame of a FLIM image is often low due to the restricted count rate requirements of TCSPC imaging, a Gaussian smoothing kernel may optionally be applied to each frame before realignment to improve the realignment.
claims.evidence: This describes an optional feature of the Galene algorithm.

claims.claim: A noticeable improvement in the realignment result was found using a smoothing kernel of width 2 or 4 pixels compared to no smoothing.
claims.source: We found a noticeable improvement in the realignment result using a kernel of with 2 or 4 pixels compared to no smoothing.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Using excessively large smoothing kernels can reduce the quality of the realignment as the contrast in the image is reduced.
claims.source: At larger kernel sizes, the correlation gradually reduced; using excessively large smoothing kernels can reduce the quality of the realignment as the contrast in the image is reduced.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of excessive smoothing and is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Using a smoothing kernel of 2–4 pixels works well over a broad range of conditions.
claims.source: We have found that using a smoothing kernel of 2–4 pixels works well over a broad range of conditions.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical testing described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Rac1 regulates a diverse array of cellular events including the cell cycle, cell-cell adhesion, motility and differentiation.
claims.source: Rac1 regulates a diverse array of cellular events including the cell cycle, cell-cell adhesion, motility and differentiation (Heasman and Ridley, 2008)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Heasman and Ridley, 2008).

claims.claim: Rac1 has been shown to be a key driver of Wnt-induced stem cell activation within the intestinal crypt.
claims.source: and has been shown to be a key driver of Wnt-induced stem cell activation within the intestinal crypt (Myant et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Myant et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The Rac1 biosensor contains an ECFP donor, which has a complex decay profile dominated by contributions from two conformations with similar spectral profiles.
claims.source: The Rac1 biosensor contains an ECFP donor, which has a complex decay profile, dominated by contributions from two conformations with similar spectral profiles.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the ECFP fluorophore.

claims.claim: The FRET efficiencies of the Rac1 GTP (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states were determined to be E = 0.65 and E = 0.02 respectively using global analysis.
claims.source: Using global analysis, we determined the FRET efficiencies of the Rac1 GTP (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states to be E = 0.65 and E = 0.02.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the data analysis performed in this work.

claims.claim: Imaging of the intestine is complicated by motion induced by peristalsis, wave-like contractions of the digestive tract which propel food through the intestine.
claims.source: Imaging of the intestine is further complicated by motion induced by peristalsis, wave-like contractions of the digestive tract which propel food through the intestine.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about intestinal physiology.

claims.claim: The gut can be attached only gently to the window as immobilizing a tract of the intestine can obstruct the bowel.
claims.source: The gut can be attached only gently to the window (Ritsma et al., 2012) as immobilizing a tract of the intestine can obstruct the bowel.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ritsma et al., 2012) and represents practical knowledge.

claims.claim: Occasional large, transient displacements occur during intestinal crypt imaging where the crypt under observation moves completely out of the field of view.
claims.source: When imaging crypts we noted that, alongside persistent smaller motion, occasional large, transient displacements occur where the crypt under observation moves completely out of the field of view (shown in the displacement estimates, Figure 4Aiii);
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Frames where the crypt moves completely out of the field of view cannot be compensated by motion correction.
claims.source: this, of course, cannot be compensated.
claims.evidence: This is a logical limitation of the motion correction approach.

claims.claim: Frames with correlation coefficient less than a threshold value (0.8) are automatically identified and removed from the reconstructed image.
claims.source: We automatically identify and remove these frames by applying a threshold to the correlation between the reference image and the best estimate of the corrected frame, in this case 0.8 (Figure 4Aiv), discarding frames with lower correlation values.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the Galene algorithm demonstrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Peristaltic motion continues even ex vivo when the intestine is maintained appropriately for live cell imaging.
claims.source: Peristaltic motion continues even ex vivo when the intestine is maintained appropriately for live cell imaging.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Scopolamine is a small molecule muscarinic antagonist that inhibits the contraction of the smooth muscle layer surrounding the intestine.
claims.source: To inhibit peristalsis for imaging, researchers often use scopolamine, a small molecule muscarinic antagonist that inhibits the contraction of the smooth muscle layer surrounding the intestine (Wang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Treatment with scopolamine effectively inhibited peristalsis in ex vivo intestinal tissue.
claims.source: Treatment with scopolamine effectively inhibited peristalsis;
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Treatment with scopolamine induced a significant activation of Rac1 in intestinal tissue compared to untreated tissue.
claims.source: however, unexpectedly we also observed a significant activation of Rac1 in tissue treated with scopolamine compared to untreated tissue (Figure 4D, quantified in E)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claims.claim: The activation of Rac1 by scopolamine was of a similar magnitude to that of tissue treated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA).
claims.source: This activation was of a similar magnitude to that of tissue treated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) (Johnsson et al., 2014), a potent small molecule activator of Rac1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and comparison to prior work.

claims.claim: The effect of scopolamine on Rac1 activation was also observed when fixed tissue was stained with a Rac1-GTP specific antibody.
claims.source: This effect was also observed when fixed tissue was stained with a Rac1-GTP specific antibody (Myant et al., 2013) (representative images and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pharmacological approaches to reducing sample motion can interfere with the biological process under observation.
claims.source: This interference with Rac1 signalling highlights the need to ensure pharmacological approaches to reducing sample motion do not affect the process under observation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that scopolamine affects Rac1 signaling.

claims.claim: Image based correction can avoid artefacts introduced by pharmacological approaches to inhibiting sample motion.
claims.source: In contrast, by using image based correction, these artefacts can be avoided when looking, for example, at subtle changes in Rac1 GTPase regulation which is known to drive stem cell activity in intestinal crypts (Myant et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between pharmacological and image-based approaches.

claims.claim: Without motion correction, it is extremely difficult to identify subcellular compartments in a majority of the intestinal crypt data.
claims.source: Without motion correction, it is extremely difficult to identify subcellular compartments in a majority of the intestinal crypt data.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: After correcting for motion, subcellular regions and structures in intestinal crypt data can be robustly identified.
claims.source: After correcting for motion, however, we are able to robustly identify subcellular regions and structures in the data.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A lower level of Rac1 activation was observed in the basal membrane compared to the apical membrane after application of PMA or scopolamine.
claims.source: We observed a lower level of Rac1 activation the basal membrane compared to the apical membrane after application of PMA or scoloplamine, suggesting a potential negative regulation of Rac1 at the basal membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The differential Rac1 activation between basal and apical membranes may be consistent with the critical role of Rac1 in intestinal crypt patterning and differentiation.
claims.source: This may be consistent with the critical role of Rac1 in intestinal crypt patterning and differentiation (de Santa Barbara et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and prior work cited.

claims.claim: Galene provides a significant improvement in the realignment of both in vivo and ex vivo imaging data compared to StackReg and SIMA.
claims.source: Galene produces a significant improvement in the image quality over SIMA and StackReg. In line with the results of our simulations and in addition to enabling correction of time resolved data, Galene demonstrates a significant improvement in the realignment of both in vivo and ex vivo imaging data.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Transient 'priming' using the pharmaceutical Rho kinase inhibitor Fasudil in a model of pancreatic cancer improved response to chemotherapy and impaired metastasis to the liver in an intrasplenic model.
claims.source: In a recent study, we demonstrated that transient 'priming' using the pharmaceutical Rho kinase inhibitor Fasudil in a model of pancreatic cancer (PC) improved response to chemotherapy and impaired metastasis to the liver in an intrasplenic model (Vennin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Vennin et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Src kinase has been shown to play a critical role in cell adhesion and proliferation in cancer.
claims.source: Src kinase has been shown to play a critical role in cell adhesion and proliferation in cancer (Brunton and Frame, 2008)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Brunton and Frame, 2008).

claims.claim: Src is potentially an anti-invasive target in pancreatic cancer.
claims.source: and is potentially an anti-invasive target in PC (Evans et al., 2012; Morton et al., 2010b; Nobis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: A reduction in Src kinase activity was previously observed in in vitro models of invasion and in end-point xenograft models of a primary tumour imaged using a skin flap technique.
claims.source: We previously observed a reduction in Src kinase activity in in vitro models of invasion and in end-point xenograft models of a primary tumour imaged using a skin flap technique.
claims.evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: The reduction in the number of metastases after priming with Fasudil could be, in part, a consequence of a reduction in early adhesion events caused by disruption of Src activation.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesised that the reduction in the number of metastases after priming with Fasudil could be, in part, a consequence of a reduction in early adhesion events caused by disruption of Src activation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior observations.

claims.claim: Without correction for sample motion, the assessment of early transient events using FRET is not possible in vivo.
claims.source: However, without correction for sample motion, the assessment of such early transient events using FRET (illustrated schematically in Figure 5B) is not possible in vivo, limiting our ability to quantify colonisation efficiency at this important stage.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations prior to using motion correction.

claims.claim: The liver shows significant motion when imaged behind an optical window due to its proximity to the lungs and heart and attachment to the diaphragm.
claims.source: The liver shows significant motion when imaged behind an optical window due to its proximity to the lungs and heart and attachment to the diaphragm.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and practical experience.

claims.claim: Motion in the liver frustrates attempts to acquire data for lifetime and hyperspectral unmixing as integration over even a few frames leads to significant image blurring.
claims.source: This frustrates attempts to acquire data for lifetime and hyperspectral unmixing as integration over even a few frames leads to significant image blurring as illustrated in Figure 5Ei.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5E showing the effect of motion on image quality.

claims.claim: A significant increase in Src activity was observed after 8 hr in cancer cells colonising the liver, which was maintained up to 16 hr before plateauing after 24 hr upon spreading.
claims.source: Here, we saw a significant increase in Src activity (increase in Src biosensor lifetime) after 8 hr, which was maintained up to 16 hr before plateauing after 24 hr upon spreading (see Figure 5E, control situation).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G.

claims.claim: Mice treated with Fasudil exhibited a significantly reduced and delayed Src activity compared to those treated with the vehicle.
claims.source: Mice treated with Fasudil exhibited a significantly reduced and delayed Src activity, in line with a delayed spreading phenotype, compared to those treated with the vehicle (see Figure 5Fi, blue-green shift at 8 hr and Figure 5Fii, blue-green shift at 24 hr, quantified in Figure 5G),
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claims.claim: Src-dependent spreading and activation during the first attachment events in the liver are impaired by treatment with Fasudil.
claims.source: indicating that Src-dependent spreading and activation during the first attachment events in the liver are indeed impaired by treatment with Fasudil.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in Src activity after Fasudil treatment.

claims.claim: Fasudil priming has a new role in altering adhesion efficiency in secondary sites.
claims.source: These results demonstrate a new role of Fasudil priming in altering adhesion efficiency in secondary sites (Rath et al., 2017; Vennin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with citations to related work.

claims.claim: There is an urgent need to develop anti-metastatic treatments in pancreatic cancer and other metastatic cancer types.
claims.source: There is an urgent need to develop anti-metastatic treatments in PC and other metastatic cancer types (Steeg, 2016)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Steeg, 2016).

claims.claim: Functional intravital microscopy combined with Galene may help development of new strategies to monitor agents that affect critical events preceding colonisation.
claims.source: and functional intravital microscopy combined with Galene may help development of new strategies to monitor agents that affect this critical event preceding colonisation (Ritsma et al., 2012; Steeg et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claims.claim: Motion during acquisition can cause blurring of the biosensor fluorescence with background autofluorescence which may have a very different lifetime, artificially changing the apparent lifetime of the biosensor.
claims.source: We note that aside from reducing the image quality, motion during acquisition can have a number of more subtle effects: (1) blurring of the biosensor fluorescence with background autofluorescence which may have a very different lifetime can artificially change the apparent lifetime of the biosensor, giving a misleading result
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion-induced blurring and is demonstrated in the data.

claims.claim: Motion can significantly distort the apparent shape of the cells.
claims.source: and (2) motion can significantly distort the apparent shape of the cells.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion during acquisition and is demonstrated in the data.

claims.claim: A reduction in the apparent lifetime of the biosensor was observed due to blurring with the low autofluorescence lifetime of surrounding liver cells.
claims.source: Both artefacts are observed here; we see a reduction in the apparent lifetime of the biosensor due to blurring with the low autofluorescence lifetime of surrounding liver cells
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing corrected and uncorrected images.

claims.claim: An artefactual elongation and apparent spreading of the cancer cell was observed due to motion.
claims.source: and an artefactual elongation and apparent spreading of the cancer cell (compare Figure 5Di–ii) which may lead to an incorrect assumption about their attachment state (see Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing corrected and uncorrected images.

claims.claim: The blurring of the biosensor lifetime with the background autofluorescence leads to an overall reduction in the lifetime in all treatment conditions when data are not motion corrected.
claims.source: The blurring of the biosensor lifetime with the background autofluorescence leads to an overall reduction in the lifetime in all treatment conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 5G and 5H.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the effect of motion on lifetime varies greatly from cell to cell depending on the motion and the environment of each cell, leading to significantly higher variance within each condition.
claims.source: As the magnitude of this effect varies greatly from cell to cell depending on the motion and the environment of each cell, we found a significantly higher degree of variance within each condition.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis comparing corrected and uncorrected data.

claims.claim: Increased variability due to motion abolishes the ability to statistically distinguish treatment conditions in Src activity measurements.
claims.source: This increased variability abolishes our ability to statistically distinguish the conditions, highlighting the importance of motion correction to obtain robust results in this context (compare in Figure 5G–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of statistical significance in Figure 5G and 5H.

claims.claim: The lifetime of NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be used as a readout of metabolic activity.
claims.source: The lifetime of NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be used as a readout of metabolic activity (Blacker and Duchen, 2016; Lakowicz et al., 1992; Skala et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Autofluorescence lifetime has potential applications in the detection of precancerous tissue.
claims.source: with potential applications in the detection of precancerous tissue.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Autofluorescence signal has been investigated in a clinical context for diagnostic purposes using static, flexible and handheld multiphoton microscopes.
claims.source: This autofluorescence signal has been investigated in a clinical context for diagnostic purposes (König, 2012) using static (Patalay et al., 2012), flexible (König et al., 2008) and handheld multiphoton (Sherlock et al., 2015) microscopes.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Unlike optical window experiments, the movement observed imaging human skin in an upright configuration occurs isotropically in three dimensions.
claims.source: Unlike optical window experiments, where the inverted imaging configuration and weight of the mouse largely constrains the sample motion to two dimensions, the movement observed imaging human skin in an upright configuration occurs isotropically in three dimensions and so correction for lateral motion alone is insufficient.
claims.evidence: This is based on practical experience and the physics of the imaging configuration.

claims.claim: Two approaches for handling motion in three dimensions are demonstrated: (1) real-time detection and compensation for axial sample motion when imaging a single plane and (2) 3D motion correction within a z-stack.
claims.source: We therefore demonstrate two approaches for handling motion in three dimensions: (1) real-time detection and compensation for axial sample motion when imaging a single plane and (2) 3D motion correction within a z-stack.
claims.evidence: This describes the approaches demonstrated in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A handheld multiphoton microscope system incorporates an active (online) axial motion compensation system that corrects for motion in z-axis in real time using OCT-based correction.
claims.source: We recently demonstrated (Sherlock et al., 2015) a handheld multiphoton microscope system that incorporates an active (online) axial motion compensation system that corrects for motion in z-axis in real time. The optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based correction system tracks sample motion perpendicular to the imaging plane in real time and adjusts the objective position to keep the selected plane in focus.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Sherlock et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The combination of active axial motion compensation and software-based lateral motion compensation with Galene is able to effectively remove the motion artefact observed in human skin imaging.
claims.source: The combination of active axial motion compensation and software-based lateral motion compensation is able to effectively remove the motion artefact observed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In a clinical setting, it is often desirable to obtain a 3D map of the autofluorescence lifetime to build up structural and functional information resolved into the strata of the skin.
claims.source: In a clinical setting, it is often desirable to obtain a 3D map of the autofluorescence lifetime to build up structural and functional information resolved into the strata of the skin, for example to quantify drug penetrance and delivery (Roberts et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Roberts et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Capturing time-resolved depth stacks with sufficient photon counts can be a time-consuming process, with a 30–50 μm stack taking 10–15 min to acquire.
claims.source: Capturing time-resolved depth stacks with sufficient photon counts can be a time-consuming process; a 30–50 μm stack may take 10–15 min to acquire.
claims.evidence: This is based on practical experience with the imaging system.

claims.claim: A certain degree of motion during 10-15 minute acquisitions is inevitable in live subjects.
claims.source: A certain degree of motion during this period is inevitable in live subjects
claims.evidence: This is a practical observation based on knowledge of live subject imaging.

claims.claim: Conventional frame-by-frame accumulation can lead to both blurring of individual images in the stack and displacement between images in the stack.
claims.source: and, since conventionally each frame is accumulated consecutively (Figure 6Bi), this can lead to both blurring of individual images in the stack and displacement between images in the stack.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion during sequential acquisition.

claims.claim: By accumulating a number of scans over the entire stack, motion in three dimensions during each stack acquisition can be estimated and corrected.
claims.source: To overcome this issue, we accumulated a number of scans over the entire stack (Figure 6Bii). We then apply the same motion estimation approach as used in 2D data, extending the displacement points to 3D. Each stack is aligned to a reference stack. Motion in three dimensions during each stack acquisition can then be estimated and corrected.
claims.evidence: This describes the approach used for 3D motion correction demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: GPU computation and algorithmic optimisations were used to reduce the processing time for correction of large 3D volumes.
claims.source: To enable correction of these large volumes, we used GPU computation and several algorithmic optimisations to reduce the processing time (see Methods, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes technical improvements made to enable 3D correction.

claims.claim: Galene is able to track and correct for motion in three dimensions during stack acquisition, obtaining undistorted deep-tissue data free from motion artefacts.
claims.source: We see that we are able to track and correct for motion in three dimensions during the stack acquisition, obtaining undistorted deep-tissue data free from motion artefacts.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The approaches demonstrated may enable the use of autofluorescence imaging of other parts of the body more susceptible to sample motion in three dimensions such as the chest.
claims.source: These approaches may enable the use of autofluorescence imaging of other parts of the body more susceptible to sample motion in three dimensions such as the chest.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claims.claim: Intravital imaging is a crucial tool in immunology, providing unique spatiotemporal information about the localisation, function and interactions between immune cells in their native environment.
claims.source: Intravital imaging is a crucial tool in immunology, providing unique spatiotemporal information about the localisation, function and interactions between immune cells in their native environment.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of intravital imaging in immunology.

claims.claim: The organisation and migration of different classes of immune cells within the lymph nodes has been shown to play a critical role in the adaptive immune response.

results.result: Galene is a versatile open-source software tool that corrects motion artifacts in FLIM and conventional fluorescence microscopy data by reconstructing individual frames from time-tagged data and using a Lucas-Kanade-based fitting approach that accounts for the raster scan pattern to estimate motion both between and within frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C22, C34-C35, C37-C39, C41-C45, C145-C146, and C170 collectively describe the core functionality and technical approach of Galene. The software's capabilities are demonstrated throughout the manuscript with multiple experimental datasets from commercial systems (Figures 1-7), and the source code availability (C170) supports reproducibility. The technical approach is well-documented with appropriate citations to prior work.

results.result: Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that Galene can effectively correct physiologically relevant motions (~10% FOV at frequencies from respiration to heartbeat), with better performance for motion along the fast scan axis than the slow axis due to differential sampling frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 and C150-C156 describe simulation results shown in Figure 2 that systematically evaluate Galene's performance across different motion parameters. The physiological reference values (C48-C49) are properly cited, and the directional dependence (C50-C51, C153-C156) is explained by the physics of laser scanning microscopy. The simulations provide quantitative benchmarks for the software's capabilities.

results.result: Galene outperforms existing motion correction packages (StackReg, SIFT, SIMA) by correcting for significantly larger sample motions, particularly for intra-frame distortions that rigid transformation methods cannot handle.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C97 are supported by comparative benchmarking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The comparison is fair as it uses the same simulated and experimental datasets across all methods. The superior performance is attributed to Galene's ability to model intra-frame motion using the scan pattern, which is a fundamental algorithmic difference from the comparison methods.

results.result: In vivo pancreatic imaging through titanium windows demonstrates that Galene successfully corrects for heartbeat-dominated motion (5.4 Hz, 27 μm) at all tested scan rates (700-1400 Hz), while larger respiration/peristalsis motion (0.2-2.2 Hz, 42 μm) requires faster scan rates (1400 Hz) for effective correction, with better performance when motion is aligned with the fast scan axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C67 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing systematic evaluation of scan rate and motion direction effects. The amplitude-spectrum analysis (C59-C60) provides quantitative characterization of the motion, and the scan rate dependence (C61-C62) is consistent with the simulation predictions. The practical recommendations (C63, C66-C67) logically follow from the experimental observations.

results.result: Optimal motion correction performance is achieved using 5-20 realignment points for 256×256 images and 10-20 points for 512×512 images, with performance degrading when using too many points due to insufficient information per point.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by empirical testing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B. The observation that performance degrades with too many realignment points (C69-C70) is logically explained by the optimization problem structure. The recommended ranges (C71) are based on systematic evaluation across multiple datasets.

results.result: Applying a Gaussian smoothing kernel of 2-4 pixels width in the fast axis improves realignment quality for low signal-to-noise FLIM data, while excessively large kernels reduce performance by decreasing image contrast.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing systematic evaluation of smoothing kernel sizes. The improvement with moderate smoothing (C73) and degradation with excessive smoothing (C74) follow logically from signal processing principles. The recommended range (C75) is based on empirical testing.

results.result: Galene enables subcellular analysis of Rac1 activity in intestinal crypts subject to peristaltic motion, revealing differential activation between basal and apical membranes, with automatic frame rejection for uncorrectable large transient displacements.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C85 and C93-C95 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-B showing successful correction of intestinal crypt imaging. The FRET efficiency determination (C79) is based on global analysis, and the subcellular analysis (C95) demonstrates the biological utility of the correction. The automatic frame rejection feature (C84) is a practical solution for uncorrectable motion (C82-C83). Background claims C76-C77 are properly cited.

results.result: Scopolamine, commonly used to inhibit peristalsis, induces significant Rac1 activation in intestinal tissue comparable to PMA treatment, demonstrating that pharmacological motion inhibition can interfere with the biological process under observation, while image-based correction avoids such artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 and C160 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing Rac1 activation by scopolamine using both FLIM-FRET and immunohistochemistry. The comparison to PMA (C89) provides context for the magnitude of the effect. This is an important finding demonstrating a key advantage of image-based correction over pharmacological approaches. The scopolamine mechanism (C86) is properly cited.

results.result: Using Galene to correct liver motion artifacts during intrasplenic metastasis imaging reveals that Fasudil priming significantly delays Src activation in cancer cells during early adhesion events (8-24 hr), providing a potential mechanism for reduced metastatic colonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C109 and C162 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing longitudinal Src-FRET imaging in the liver. The prior work on Fasudil (C98) is properly cited, and the hypothesis (C102) is tested with appropriate controls. The significant delay in Src activity (C107) is demonstrated with statistical analysis (Figure 5G), and the conclusion about adhesion efficiency (C108-C109) is supported by the data. Background claims C99-C101 are properly cited.

results.result: Motion during acquisition introduces significant artifacts in FLIM-FRET measurements by blurring biosensor fluorescence with background autofluorescence and distorting cell morphology, leading to reduced apparent lifetimes and increased variability that abolishes statistical power to distinguish treatment conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 and C161 are supported by comparison of corrected and uncorrected data in Figure 5D-H. The specific artifacts observed (C114-C115) are documented, and the quantitative impact on statistical analysis (C116-C118) is demonstrated by comparing Figure 5G (corrected, significant differences) with Figure 5H (uncorrected, no significant differences). This demonstrates the critical importance of motion correction for quantitative FLIM analysis.

results.result: Galene successfully corrects 3D motion in human skin autofluorescence imaging by combining active axial motion compensation with software-based lateral correction for single planes, or by accumulating multiple stack acquisitions and extending the 2D displacement estimation to 3D, with GPU acceleration enabling practical processing times.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C132 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 demonstrating two approaches for 3D motion correction in human skin. The combination of hardware and software correction (C125) is shown in Figure 6A, and the stack-based 3D correction (C130, C132) is shown in Figure 6C. The GPU acceleration (C131, C148) is documented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. Background claims C119, C121, C124, C126 are properly cited.

results.result: Galene provides superior motion correction for 3D multispectral imaging of immune cells in lymph nodes compared to Imaris drift correction, maintaining high correlation of static structures over 30 minutes despite slow drift and respiratory motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C36 and C135-C144 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7 comparing Galene to Imaris drift correction for lymph node imaging. The quantitative comparison (C141-C143) shows Galene maintains higher correlation with static structures (Figure 7E-F). This demonstrates Galene's applicability beyond FLIM to conventional fluorescence microscopy. Background claims C135-C137 are properly cited or represent established knowledge.

results.result: GPU acceleration and exploitation of the banded Hessian matrix structure reduce 3D motion correction processing time by a factor of 30 for typical volumetric datasets, enabling potential future online correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149 are supported by timing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C showing the computational improvements. The 30-fold speedup (C148) is quantitatively demonstrated, and the technical approaches (GPU acceleration and banded factorization) are clearly described in the Methods. The speculation about future online correction (C149) is reasonable given the demonstrated performance.

results.result: Galene enables FLIM imaging in previously inaccessible contexts by correcting for physiological motion in intravital imaging of murine abdominal organs and human skin autofluorescence, rescuing previously discarded data and relaxing restrictions on sample stability and imaging duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C157-C158, and C168-C169 represent summary conclusions supported by the collective experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript (Figures 3-7). The ability to resolve images in challenging contexts (C5-C6) is demonstrated with multiple biological systems, and the practical impact (C7-C8, C169) logically follows from the demonstrated capabilities. These are appropriate summary statements of the work's significance.

results.result: Background and motivation: FLIM and FRET-based biosensors provide valuable functional readouts in intravital microscopy, but long acquisition times required for sufficient signal make them susceptible to motion artifacts from physiological processes, while existing motion correction approaches have not been applied to FLIM data due to conventional histogram accumulation methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C33 provide background context and motivation for the work. These claims are either established knowledge in the field (C1-C3, C15, C17-C18, C23-C25, C28) or properly cited to prior work (C9-C14, C26-C27, C29, C32). The statement about prior work not being applied to FLIM (C30-C31) establishes the novelty of the current work. These background claims appropriately frame the problem being addressed.

results.result: Speculation about potential applications: The authors speculate that Galene may enable various future applications including imaging other body regions, other FRET biosensors, endoscopic systems, and combination with hardware motion correction, though these remain to be demonstrated.
results.evaluation: Claims C96, C102, C110-C111, C120, C133, C159, C163-C164, C166-C167 represent speculations about potential future applications. While these are reasonable extrapolations from the demonstrated capabilities, they have not been experimentally validated in this work. The speculation is appropriately qualified in most cases (e.g., 'may', 'could', 'potential'), but these claims cannot be evaluated as supported without additional data.

results.result: Processing time for motion correction is typically significantly shorter than data acquisition, even for high-speed 3D applications, enabling potential real-time correction.
results.evaluation: Claim C165 is supported by the timing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C showing that even complex 3D corrections can be completed in minutes. Combined with the 30-fold speedup from GPU acceleration (C148), this supports the feasibility of real-time correction, though actual real-time implementation is not demonstrated.
